tldr: Instead of leaving task progression and coordinate correction entirely to the VLA, this paper dramatically stabilizes long-horizon loco-manipulation by offloading them to classical control: a predicate-based state machine and world-coordinate locking.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed PGX framework. The top-layer predicate-based finite state machine (FSM) governs phase transitions and recovery based on physical events, the middle-layer VLA executes local manipulation skills, and the bottom-layer world-coordinate locking (WCL) suppresses base sway and drift to ensure spatial precision.
overview:
Long-horizon loco-manipulation, such as a humanoid walking around an indoor space, operating a coffee machine, and delivering a cup, is one of the grand goals in robotics. In recent years, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that directly output actions from images and language have advanced remarkably. However, relying on a single monolithic, flat policy to handle locomotion, manipulation, timing decisions, and millimeter-level precision all at once has proven impractical. Foot sway causes the end-effector coordinates to drift, visually similar scenes lead to phase confusion, and the model often stalls during manipulation because walking and idle states dominate the training data.

To address this, the authors shifted their perspective: time and space constraints ("when and where to act") can be delegated to classical mechanisms grounded in physical quantities, allowing the VLA to focus solely on learning "how to manipulate"—the local skill dynamics it naturally excels at. This is the core concept of Physically Grounded Execution (PGX). PGX consists of three layers: a state machine that manages phase transitions and retries via physical predicates, a VLA skill execution module, and world-coordinate locking (WCL) that compensates for base drift and target positions within the world frame.

Extensive evaluations across three simulated tasks (box transport, mug placement, coffee fetching) in Isaac Lab Arena and on a real-world Unitree G1 humanoid robot showed massive performance improvements. Without modifying any model weights of state-of-the-art VLAs ($\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.6), the success rate on the coffee-fetching task jumped from 35% to 80%.
contributions: Proposed PGX, a training-free execution framework that cleanly decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: temporal progression (FSM), local skills (VLA), and spatial precision (WCL).

Defined a unified physical predicate interface shared across offline demonstration segmentation, online transition gating, and stage-wise evaluation, enabling phase disambiguation as well as recovery and reverse transitions.
Developed world-coordinate locking (WCL) to absorb bipedal humanoid sway and drift through object-relative stance positioning, base station keeping, and world-anchored contact targets.
Demonstrated on three simulation tasks and a real humanoid robot (Unitree G1) that long-horizon tasks can be successfully completed without altering existing VLA model weights.

sections.heading: Why asking a single VLA model to do everything hits a wall
sections.summary: Tackling long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation with a single monolithic VLA model fails due to a loss of temporal structure, coordinate drift from foot sway, and severe data imbalance. This paper introduces PGX, which offloads "when and where to act" to lightweight physical mechanisms, letting the VLA focus strictly on manipulation skills.
sections.details:
Humanoids operating in domestic or logistics environments must handle long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks that combine multiple stages of walking locomotion and precision contact manipulation. However, attempting to solve this with a single end-to-end policy runs into three major obstacles.

First is the "loss of temporal structure." Relying solely on visual observations makes it difficult to track task progress, leading the model to select incorrect actions in visually similar but temporally distinct phases. Second is "reference frame drift." Every time a humanoid steps or walks, its pelvis (base) frame moves, making millimeter-level precision positioning of the hand exceptionally hard. Third is "data imbalance." Most data in long-horizon demonstrations consist of walking or standing still, which biases training toward conservative behaviors and causes the policy to hesitate during critical contact manipulation.

Classical approaches like Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) are rigorous, but they struggle with environmental variation and complex contact, requiring every skill to be hand-engineered. VLAs, on the other hand, learn flexible and generalizable skills, but asking a neural network to internally resolve long-horizon temporal scheduling and millimeter-level geometric precision is highly inefficient.

The central insight here is that "when to act" (timing) and "where to anchor actions" (precision) can be derived directly from physical quantities, whereas the true strength of a VLA lies in "how to manipulate" (skills) during local contact. PGX clarifies this division of responsibility, using a thin, training-free execution layer to dramatically unlock the capabilities of existing VLA backbones.

captions.F1: Comparison on the long-horizon humanoid coffee-fetching task. A flat monolithic VLA triggers the wrong skill in front of the machine and fails, whereas PGX successfully completes all 8 stages by offloading timing and spatial precision.

sections.heading: At the intersection of whole-body control, long-horizon VLAs, and hybrid execution
sections.summary: Prior work has focused on improving whole-body controllers, using large models for subtask planning, or adding internal memory to policies. PGX diverges by taking a hybrid control approach, supporting the VLA with an explicit state machine and world-coordinate locking grounded in physical states and events.
sections.details:
### Humanoid Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation
Humanoid control has advanced rapidly thanks to reinforcement learning-based Whole-Body Controllers (WBC), enabling precise tracking of teleoperation and motion imitation data. While mounting generalist VLAs on top of WBCs is gaining traction, most existing research focuses either on refining the controllers themselves or expanding training datasets, leaving the challenge of structuring long-horizon workflows largely unaddressed.

### Long-Horizon Manipulation with VLAs
There are three main approaches to tackling long-horizon tasks with VLAs. The first uses LLMs or VLMs as high-level planners to infer the current subtask from images. The second incorporates explicit memory modules or action chunking into the policy architecture to enhance temporal representations. The third chains separately trained skills by normalizing the terminal state of one skill into the initial state of the next. However, because these methods rely on probabilistic neural network inference for skill switching, perceptual errors can cause catastrophic failures. PGX fundamentally differs by anchoring skill transitions to physical events rather than semantic inference.

### Structured Execution and Hybrid Control
Combining symbolic state machines or behavior trees with continuous control has a long history in robotics. Recently, the importance of initial stance positioning has been highlighted in wheeled mobile manipulators. However, unlike wheeled bases, bipedal humanoids inherently sway and drift even while standing still. PGX absorbs this biped-specific instability, serving as a practical bridge between learned skills and whole-body controllers.

sections.heading: Dividing the labor across three layers: predicate state machine, VLA skills, and world-coordinate locking
sections.summary: PGX consists of three layers: a finite state machine (FSM) that strictly manages phases via physical predicates, a VLA that executes local manipulation, and world-coordinate locking (WCL) that suppresses drift and aligns coordinates. Sharing identical physical predicates across offline data segmentation and online execution is key.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation
A long-horizon task is formulated as a directed graph $\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{E})$. Robot observations comprise standard policy inputs $o_t$ (camera images, joint angles) and executor state $z_t$ obtained from state estimation, such as base position and grasp state. The VLA outputs an action chunk of horizon $H$ based on image and text instructions. PGX does not modify the VLA's internal parameters $	heta$ at all; it acts as a runtime wrapper that selects, constrains, or overrides action channels at each control step.

### III-B Predicate-Gated State Machine
Each stage $s_k$ is defined by a tuple: instruction text, designated executor, completion predicate (guard), timeout, and retry policy. Walking and waiting are delegated to navigation and timers, allowing the VLA to focus exclusively on active manipulation stages. Phase completion is governed by five primitive predicates: grasped, placed, triggered, at-stance, and dropped. For example, grasped fires only when hand closure, wrist-to-object distance, and object lift height are all satisfied, preventing false detections of missed grasps. Temporal hysteresis (holding the condition for a threshold duration) is applied to guard against sensor noise.
A crucial design principle is that offline demonstration segmentation, online phase transitions, and evaluation progress tracking all share the exact same predicate definitions. The FSM also incorporates physical recovery mechanisms, such as stance resets upon timeout and reverse transitions—for instance, returning to the placement stage if the robot accidentally re-grasps the mug during the button-pressing phase.

### III-C Skill Execution via Fine-Tuned VLAs
Immediately before the VLA executes a skill, the executor drives the base to an appropriate relative stance and resets the arms to an initial configuration (such as a ready or carrying pose). This aligns the skill's initial conditions between training and deployment. The framework accommodates both "flat models" trained across full demonstrations and "stage models" trained exclusively on manipulation segments extracted by the shared predicates.

### III-D World-Coordinate Locking (WCL)
To counter base sway and drift, spatial references are anchored in the world coordinate frame. WCL comprises three main components:
- **Object-Relative Stance**: Target stance poses are updated relative to the detected object's current position rather than fixed map coordinates, preventing upstream placement errors from compounding into downstream failures.
- **Base Station Keeping**: During multi-step manipulation at the same workstation, a deadband controller activates corrections if base pelvis drift exceeds an outer threshold and deactivates once it returns within an inner threshold. Base velocity commands from the VLA are masked during manipulation to eliminate spurious foot movements.
- **World-Anchored Contact Targets**: Millimeter-precision contact goals, such as pushing a button, are maintained in the world frame $W$ and reprojected into the latest base frame $B$ at each control step for inverse kinematics (IK) arm control. This ensures the end-effector tracks a fixed point in space even if the feet sway.

captions.F2: Detailed architecture of PGX. The FSM (top) manages predicate guards, retries, and reverse transitions; the VLA (middle) executes visual skills from standardized initial states; and WCL (bottom) handles base station keeping and IK-based target tracking in the world frame.

sections.heading: Success rates soar without touching the VLA weights
sections.summary: Evaluations using $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.6 across three simulation tasks and the real Unitree G1 robot showed massive gains. PGX achieved high success rates even under randomized initial poses where flat VLAs failed almost completely, with ablations confirming the critical impact of WCL.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
Simulation experiments were conducted in Isaac Lab Arena using a Unitree G1 humanoid equipped with Dex-3 hands across three tasks: bimanual "Box transport," single-arm "Mug placement," and the most challenging "Coffee fetching" (an 8-stage sequence: grasp $	o$ carry to machine $	o$ place $	o$ press button $	o$ re-grasp $	o$ serve). Backbones included $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.6 paired with whole-body controllers (HOMIE and GR00T-WBC). Tests evaluated nominal initial poses (C0) alongside a randomized setting (C1) with position perturbations of $\pm 0.30$ m and yaw variations of $\pm 30^{\circ}$.

### IV-B Long-Horizon Task: Coffee Fetching
A flat $\pi_{0.5}$ policy bypassed the coffee machine entirely and walked straight to the serving tray, resulting in a 0% success rate. Wrapping it with PGX yielded a 60% success rate under nominal conditions and 55% under randomized positions. The result with GR00T was even more striking: without changing any model weights, PGX boosted its success rate from 35% to 80% (nominal) and from 20% to 80% (randomized). While the state machine alone achieved a 90–95% mug lift rate, adding world-coordinate locking (WCL) drastically increased the button-press success rate, lifting overall task completion by up to 28 percentage points.

### IV-C Multi-Task Generalization
Similar dramatic improvements were observed in box transport and mug placement. Across all six experimental configurations (3 tasks $	imes$ 2 conditions), the average stage progression and success rate more than doubled—rising from 35% to 78% for GR00T and from 17% to 82% for $\pi_{0.5}$. Under randomized initial conditions, flat policies failed even the initial grasp due to unseen visual perspectives, whereas PGX autonomously regained an object-relative stance via navigation, suffering almost no performance drop.

### IV-D Execution Structure vs. Stage-Wise Training
To determine whether the gains stemmed from stage-wise model fine-tuning or from the PGX execution structure itself, the authors deployed a single flat model under PGX using a fixed, global task prompt. This configuration recovered the vast majority of the performance gains, demonstrating that execution-level initial state guarantees and physical guards—rather than language instruction switching—are the primary drivers of success.

### IV-E Efficacy of World-Coordinate Locking (WCL)
Disabling WCL led to a substantial drop in coffee-fetching success (from 80% to 65% with GR00T). In stress tests injecting artificial base displacement noise every 3 seconds during manipulation, the 90th-percentile maximum base drift reached 54 cm without station keeping, causing task failure. With WCL, drift remained contained within 9 cm.

### IV-F Real Humanoid Experiments
Using a physical Unitree G1 robot with Vicon motion capture for predicate verification, the team deployed the full coffee-fetching task. The humanoid reliably executed the complete sequence—from grasping and placing in the machine to re-grasping and serving—confirming that the stage structure developed in simulation transfers directly to the real world.

sections.heading: Bridging foundation models and classical control for the future of humanoids
sections.summary: PGX significantly boosts the long-horizon loco-manipulation capabilities of existing VLA models through training-free classical techniques: a predicate state machine and world-coordinate locking. Future work includes reducing execution latency during phase transitions and expanding the skill repertoire.
sections.details:
This paper decomposes the challenges of long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation into three distinct pillars—temporal structure, manipulation skills, and geometric precision—and introduces the PGX framework to coordinate them effectively.

Using a state machine governed by physical events to resolve "when to act," anchoring "where to act" in the world frame via object-relative stances and station keeping, and leaving the VLA to handle only "how to act" during local manipulation transforms catastrophic failure rates into practical success—all without retraining state-of-the-art VLA models. Validated in both simulation and on a physical humanoid, this work offers compelling insights into how robot foundation models should interface with classical planning and control.

A recognized limitation is task execution time: waiting for predicates to settle, dampening stopping transients, and executing safe stance resets increase total cycle time compared to end-to-end execution. Accelerating stage transitions and scaling to more diverse, dynamic skills remain promising directions for future research.

takeaways: Relying on a VLA to handle overall task timing and millimeter-level coordinate precision is an anti-pattern; offloading physically grounded requirements to classical control is far more effective.

Strictly sharing identical physical predicates across offline data segmentation, online transition gating, and evaluation perfectly aligns the policy's training distribution with its execution conditions.
Because bipedal humanoids sway and drift even while manipulating objects, base station keeping and object-relative stances in the world frame are critical for high success rates.
Rather than forcing large foundation models into an end-to-end paradigm, wrapping them in a principled control architecture unlocks multiples of their baseline performance using existing weights.
limitations: Overall task duration is longer than pure end-to-end policies due to predicate verification delays, settling times for base sway, and safe reset sequences.
Predicate evaluation depends partially on reliable state estimation pipelines, such as grasp detection, object pose tracking, and real-world motion capture.
The task graph (stage ordering and guard conditions) is currently authored manually rather than generated automatically for novel tasks.
